analysis.one_liner: Bans the production, sale, use, import, or export of the herbicide atrazine, with criminal penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a floor vote: introduced with no cosponsors in 2007, it was shuttled among four House committees and its subcommittees and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a crime, punishable by fines or up to two years in prison, to use, make, sell, import, or export any pesticide containing atrazine, a weed killer sprayed heavily on corn and other row crops. The purpose of such a ban is to keep atrazine out of drinking water and the environment; the European Union already banned it in 2003, while the United States instead regulates how much may remain in water. The bill got a hearing-free referral path and no cosponsors, and it never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that drink from public water systems in farm country, where atrazine regularly shows up in surface and groundwater, especially in spring after cornfields are sprayed. Farmworkers and rural residents closest to sprayed fields would also benefit, as would aquatic ecosystems, since atrazine at low concentrations is linked to endocrine effects in frogs and fish. Municipal water systems would benefit by avoiding the cost of filtering atrazine out of raw water.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural drinking-water households and water utilities

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits every use, production, sale, importation, and exportation of atrazine or any pesticide containing it, removing the herbicide from the market entirely rather than capping residues.
Enforces the ban with criminal penalties — a fine or up to two years in prison, or both — rather than relying solely on civil pesticide-enforcement procedures.

analysis.who_pays: Atrazine manufacturers — above all Syngenta, which makes the country's leading atrazine products — would lose their dominant herbicide line. Corn and sorghum growers would pay for alternative weed control, and there is no cheaper broadleaf herbicide with atrazine's price point, so food-production costs could edge up. Farmers who stockpiled product or built their weed-control programs around it would face abrupt disruption, with criminal liability attached to continued use.

drawbacks.text: Corn, sorghum, and sugarcane farmers lose the cheapest and most widely used broadleaf weed killer, raising weed-control costs on tens of millions of acres with no obvious one-for-one substitute.

The bill reaches the entire supply chain with criminal penalties of up to two years in prison, which is a blunter instrument than the EPA's existing system of registration limits, application restrictions, and a legal water-contamination standard that many growers view as adequate.
The ban takes effect without any phase-out or compensation for farmers who planned rotations around atrazine and for dealers holding inventory.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health and environmental case is real: atrazine is one of the most commonly detected pesticides in US waterways, the EU banned it for exactly the water-contamination reason, and the people bearing the exposure are concentrated in farming regions rather than spread across the country. But the bill as written is abrupt — a same-day criminal ban with no phase-out, no substitute program for growers, and a penalty scheme aimed down the supply chain. A designed version would probably have paired the ban with a transition period; this one asks farmers to absorb the full cost overnight, which helps explain why it drew no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee referrals and subcommittees for the rest of the Congress, never got a cosponsor or a hearing, and expired when the session ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on August 3, 2007, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and additionally to Ways and Means and Foreign Affairs.
It was immediately routed to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials rather than taken up by the full committee.

On September 29, 2008, the bill was rereferred so the Agriculture Committee was listed first, with Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Foreign Affairs also holding it, and it was then sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Atrazine manufacturers and farmers who kept using the herbicide are better off: no restriction was enacted, and water systems and rural residents continue to bear the exposure and the treatment costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Atrazine makers and the farmers who spray it

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pursued a rereference to more committees, including Agriculture, in 2008; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House subcommittees of referral
against.role: Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials, then Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in subcommittee — first on environment, then on health after rereference — without a hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Atrazine manufacturers, led by Syngenta
against.what_they_did: The leading atrazine manufacturer actively defended the product against restriction through this period, funding research and lobbying to keep it registered; no restriction passed.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the record shows only one Democrat acting alone with no recorded partisan opposition — the bill simply never advanced.

industries.industry: Atrazine herbicide manufacturers (Syngenta and other registrants)
industries.note: A total ban eliminates the US market for atrazine products outright, including export sales, which the bill also prohibits. The industry's interest in keeping the product registered runs against the interest of households and water systems that pay to keep atrazine out of their water.

Farmers would lose the cheapest weed-killer for corn and face criminal penalties for any remaining use. Many are also the rural residents whose wells and streams carry atrazine, so the industry's interest and the public's are partly aligned and partly opposed.
Utilities in corn-growing regions would no longer have to test for and remove atrazine from source water under EPA's legal limit, saving treatment costs their ratepayers bear.
